lessons.title: Pricing Futures — Cost of Carry, Contango, and Backwardation

children.text: On 20 April 2020, MCX settled its expiring April crude oil contract at minus ₹2,884 per barrel. Not a low price, a negative one: sellers effectively had to pay buyers to take barrels off their hands. This happened because, on the same day in New York, WTI crude's expiring May contract collapsed to about minus $37.63 a barrel as the world ran out of places to physically store oil during the pandemic demand collapse. Since MCX crude oil is cash-settled against a rupee-converted WTI price, that global storage crisis flowed straight into Indian traders' accounts, even though not one of them ever touched a barrel. To understand how a price can go negative, and why futures prices normally sit above or below spot prices at all, you need the cost-of-carry model. That is what this lesson builds.

body.text: A futures price is not a prediction of where spot prices are headed. In its simplest form, it is the spot price today, adjusted for the net cost of carrying that commodity forward to the contract's expiry: financing cost and storage cost, minus the benefit of holding the physical commodity right now.

markDefs.definition: The benefit of physically holding a commodity right now rather than owning a promise to receive it later, such as being able to keep a factory running during a supply shortage. It is the one term in the cost-of-carry model that pulls the futures price down.

children.text: Imagine two ways to own gold three months from now. Buy it today and hold it, paying financing cost and storage until then. Or simply buy a three-month futures contract today and take delivery later. In a well-functioning market, both routes should cost roughly the same, otherwise everyone would pile into the cheaper one until prices adjusted. That logic gives the cost-of-carry formula. Financing cost and storage cost push the futures price above spot, since holding the commodity yourself ties up capital and costs money to store. Working against that is the
, the value of having the physical commodity in hand right now rather than a paper claim on it later.

body.caption: F = futures price, S = spot price, r = financing (interest) rate, u = storage cost rate, y = convenience yield rate, t = time to expiry in years. A simplified, discretely-compounded version of the cost-of-carry model.
How the cost-of-carry terms typically behave, by commodity type

cells: Meaningful; capital tied up earns no interest elsewhere
Low; a vault charges comparatively little to store metal
Can be high and can even spike sharply, as storage tanks or warehouses fill up

children.text: Contango: The Normal State for Storable Commodities

markDefs.definition: A market condition where the futures price is higher than the spot price (and longer-dated contracts are priced higher than nearer-dated ones), typically because financing and storage costs outweigh any convenience yield.

children.text: Because gold has almost no convenience yield, it sits in
almost all the time: the futures price sits above spot, by roughly the cost of financing and storing it until expiry.

body.title: Price a 3-month gold future
body.prompt: MCX Gold spot-equivalent price is ₹60,000 per 10 grams. Assume a combined annual financing and storage cost of 7.5%, and a convenience yield of 0% (a reasonable assumption for gold). Using the simplified cost-of-carry formula, what is the fair 3-month (0.25 year) futures price, rounded to the nearest rupee?
body.explanation: F = 60,000 × (1 + 0.075 × 0.25) = 60,000 × 1.01875 = ₹61,125. The ₹1,125 premium over spot is the cost of carrying gold forward three months, nothing more mysterious than financing plus storage.

children.text: Backwardation: When Now Is Worth More Than Later

markDefs.definition: A market condition where the futures price is lower than the spot price (and nearer-dated contracts are priced higher than longer-dated ones), typically because convenience yield, the value of having physical supply right now, outweighs financing and storage costs.

children.text: When convenience yield rises enough to outweigh financing and storage cost, the relationship flips into

: spot trades above futures. Picture jeera just before harvest, when existing stock is thin and processors need physical supply immediately, while the post-harvest contract, expecting a wave of fresh supply, trades cheaper. Or picture crude oil during a genuine supply crunch, when refiners will pay up for oil they can use today over a promise of oil next month.

columns.label: Contango
points: Farther-dated contracts price higher than nearer ones
Driven by financing and storage cost exceeding convenience yield
The normal state for gold and silver

columns.label: Backwardation
points: Nearer-dated contracts price higher than farther ones
Driven by convenience yield (physical scarcity) exceeding financing and storage cost
Common in crude oil and agri commodities during supply tightness

children.text: The Day Storage Cost Went Through the Roof: MCX Crude Oil, 20 April 2020

Contango exists because storage costs money. Take that logic to its extreme, and you get 20 April 2020. Storage tanks at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for WTI crude, were running out of room as pandemic lockdowns crushed fuel demand overnight. Anyone still holding a long position in the expiring WTI contract who had not arranged storage faced a stark choice: pay an exorbitant, possibly unavailable storage fee, or pay someone else to take the oil, and the contract, off their hands. Storage cost, the 'u' in the cost-of-carry formula, effectively spiked so high that the fair price for that expiring contract went negative.

body.title: 20 April 2020, and its aftermath in India

events.title: MCX trading closes at 5 PM
events.description: SEBI had shortened MCX's trading hours to 5 PM because of pandemic-related market conditions, versus the usual 11:30 PM close. Traders in MCX crude oil could not react to news that broke after that.

events.title: WTI crashes to about minus $37.63
events.description: With Cushing storage essentially full, the expiring May WTI contract in New York collapses into deeply negative territory, a first in its history.

events.title: MCX settles at minus ₹2,884 per barrel
events.description: Since MCX crude oil is cash-settled off a rupee-converted WTI reference price, the exchange settles its own expiring April contract at a negative price to maintain consistency with the global benchmark. Estimated losses across Indian traders, heavily retail, run to roughly ₹450 crore.

events.title: Brokers challenge the settlement
events.description: Motilal Oswal, PCS Securities and Religare separately petition the Bombay High Court against MCX and SEBI over the negative settlement price.

events.title: The settlement price is upheld
events.description: The court dismisses the challenges, holding that participants in derivatives markets knowingly take on commercial risk and cannot seek judicial reversal simply because a market move produced large losses.

body.text: 'Cash-settled' does not mean 'insulated from physical-market chaos.' MCX crude oil traders never touched a barrel of oil, yet a storage crunch half the world away still determined their settlement price in rupees. Global benchmark linkage cuts both ways: it gives you a transparent, liquid market, and it also imports risks you cannot see forming in your own country.

children.text: Roll Yield: Why Holding a Futures Position Isn't Like Holding a Stock

markDefs.definition: The gain or loss that comes purely from rolling a futures position from an expiring contract into a later-dated one, separate from any change in the spot price itself.

children.text: A trader (or a commodity fund) who wants continuous exposure without ever taking delivery must roll from the expiring contract into a later one, and whether that roll is a cost or a gain, the
, depends entirely on which state the market is in.

body.caption: Roll yield for a long position rolling from a near-month to a far-month contract
headers: Effect of rolling a long position

cells: Far-month contract priced higher than near-month
You sell the cheaper expiring contract and buy the costlier far-month one: a roll cost, a negative roll yield
Far-month contract priced lower than near-month
You sell the costlier expiring contract and buy the cheaper far-month one: a roll gain, a positive roll yield

body.text: This is precisely why a crude oil futures fund can lose money over a year even when spot crude oil ends the year unchanged: persistent contango quietly taxes every roll. Chapter 4 covers calendar spreads, the strategy built directly on trading this near-month versus far-month gap.

body.title: Spot the market state
body.question: Jeera is trading at ₹22,000 per quintal in the spot market. The nearest futures contract trades at ₹21,500, and a contract three months further out trades at ₹20,900, reflecting expectations of a large new harvest. What is this market in?
options: Contango, because prices are falling over time
Backwardation, because spot and near-month prices are above the far-month price
Neither, since agricultural commodities cannot be in backwardation
Contango, because futures always price above spot for agricultural commodities
body.explanation: Spot and near-month prices sit above the far-month price, the definition of backwardation. It fits the story too: current supply is relatively tight (pushing up the convenience yield of holding physical jeera now), while an expected large harvest is pulling the more distant contract's price down.

cards.definition: The net cost of holding a commodity from today until a future date: financing cost plus storage cost, minus convenience yield.
The benefit of holding a physical commodity right now rather than a claim to receive it later.
A market state where futures trade above spot, and farther-dated contracts trade above nearer ones.
A market state where futures trade below spot, and nearer-dated contracts trade above farther ones.
The gain or loss from rolling a futures position into a later-dated contract, separate from any change in spot price; negative in contango, positive in backwardation.

points: A futures price is the spot price adjusted for the net cost of carrying the commodity forward: financing and storage cost, minus convenience yield.

Gold and silver, with near-zero convenience yield, sit in contango almost all the time. Crude oil and agricultural commodities can swing between contango and backwardation as physical scarcity changes.

On 20 April 2020, an extreme storage shortage at Cushing pushed WTI crude, and consequently MCX's rupee-linked crude oil contract, to a negative settlement price, a direct real-world consequence of storage cost overwhelming everything else in the cost-of-carry model.
Rolling a long futures position costs you in contango and pays you in backwardation, which is why long-term commodity futures exposure rarely behaves exactly like holding the physical commodity.
Cash settlement removes delivery risk for you personally, but it does not remove your exposure to whatever is happening in the global physical market underlying the benchmark price.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Cost-of-carry examples use illustrative, simplified figures. Actual futures pricing reflects live market conditions, financing rates and exchange-specific factors that can differ from this simplified model.
